content: The Cheroot, also known as the Stogie, is a type of cigar that is cylindrical in shape and has both ends clipped during the manufacturing process. Unlike tapered cigars, cheroots are easier and less expensive to produce mechanically, which contributes to their affordability and popularity.5 and 6.5 inches in length and have a ring gauge of 34 to 37. For reference, a stogie has a diameter slightly greater than half an inch. The term stogie is often misapplied to describe any cigar with an unpleasant odor. Many stogies are made using flavored tobaccos, and because they can be smoked for approximately 30 minutes—much longer than the 2 to 8 minutes it takes to smoke a cigarette—they can produce a strong and lingering smell. The word stogie is derived from Conestoga, referencing the Conestoga Valley in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, where these cigars were popular among teamsters driving Conestoga wagons. The term cheroot originates from the French word cheroute, which itself is derived from the Tamil words curuttu, churuttu, or shuruttu, meaning roll of tobacco. This Tamil term likely entered the French language during the early 16th century, when the French were establishing a presence in South India, and was later adopted into English. Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain, was frequently photographed smoking stogies. Despite his fondness for cigars, his wife disapproved of the habit, which he often joked about. During one of his lectures, Twain humorously claimed that he paid $5 per barrel for his cigars because of his incurable extravagance. In a letter dated 1905, later quoted in the March 26, 1911 edition of the New York Times, Twain wrote, I know a good cigar better than you do, for I have had sixty years' experience. No, that is not what I mean; I mean I know a bad cigar better than anybody else. I judge by the price only; if it costs above 5 cents, I know it to be either foreign or half foreign and unsmokable. Twain also mentioned that he owned many boxes of Havana cigars, ranging in price from 20 cents to $1.66 each, all of which were gifts. He admitted that he had never smoked any of them and never intended to, instead reserving them for visitors. In modern times, notable stogie enthusiasts include radio host Rush Limbaugh and filmmaker Francis Ford Coppola, who even sells his own private-label stogies at his winery. Singer Roger Miller, known for his love of smoking, referenced stogies in his song King of the Road with the lyrics: I smoke old stogies I have found / Short, but not too big around. Cheroots have a historical connection to Asia, particularly Burma (now Myanmar) and India, where they have been traditionally popular. During the British Empire, cheroots gained favor among the British, and they are often associated with Burma in literature. Interestingly, cheroot smoking was once linked to resistance against tropical diseases in India. Verrier Elwin, in the foreword to his 1957 book Leaves from the Jungle: Life in a Gond Village, noted that he frequently fell ill during his early years as a non-smoker. However, after taking up cheroot smoking, he claimed to have avoided further bouts of malaria and experienced significant improvements in his overall health. He attributed this to the cheroot's aroma, which may have masked the scent of sweat that attracts mosquitoes, thereby reducing the likelihood of mosquito bites and subsequent malaria transmission.
